sec.title: Purpose
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis quantitatively synthesized the available evidence on the association between periodontal disease (PD) and the risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ). We also examined whether MRONJ risk varied according to PD severity among patients receiving antiresorptive or antiangiogenic therapy.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: MEDLINE, Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, and Google Scholar were comprehensively searched for studies published through November 30, 2025, in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Eligible studies were required to provide a reproducible definition of PD based on clinical, radiographic, guideline-based, or predefined administrative-code criteria. Studies relying on non-operationalized clinical labels without sufficient diagnostic detail were excluded. A random-effects meta-analysis was performed using log-transformed relative-effect estimates and their standard errors. To address heterogeneity in exposure definitions, studies were stratified into a severe/procedure-linked group and a moderate-to-mixed group.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Eight observational studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in the quantitative synthesis. The primary meta-analysis showed a statistically significant association between PD and MRONJ, indicating that patients with PD had an approximately threefold higher risk of developing MRONJ than those without PD (pooled relative-effect estimate, 3.02; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.99–4.56). In subgroup analyses, the severe/procedure-linked group had a higher pooled relative-effect estimate (4.26; 95% CI, 1.96–9.24) than the moderate-to-mixed group (2.39; 95% CI, 1.45–3.94). However, the between-subgroup difference was not statistically significant; therefore, the subgroup findings should be interpreted as exploratory.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Current evidence supports an association between PD and increased MRONJ risk in patients receiving antiresorptive or antiangiogenic therapy. Although the subgroup findings suggest that more advanced periodontal breakdown may be associated with greater risk, this severity-based pattern should be interpreted cautiously and confirmed in future studies with larger sample sizes and standardized diagnostic criteria.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ) is defined as exposed maxillofacial bone, or bone that can be probed through an intraoral or extraoral fistula, persisting for >8 weeks in patients with a history of antiresorptive or antiangiogenic therapy and no history of jaw radiation [1]. First identified in 2003 among patients with cancer receiving bisphosphonates, MRONJ is now recognized as an iatrogenic condition affecting patients worldwide [2]. Although its prevalence is low, its recalcitrant clinical course poses a substantial challenge for clinicians, underscoring the need to identify risk factors and establish effective preventive strategies [3]. Among recognized local risk factors, invasive dental procedures, particularly tooth extractions, are the most important precipitating events [456]. However, the role of preexisting oral pathologies, especially periodontal disease (PD), as independent risk factors remains under investigation [78].

PD is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by destruction of the tooth-supporting structures, including the alveolar bone [910]. A biological link between PD and MRONJ is plausible because the chronic inflammatory burden and bacterial biofilm associated with PD may create a microenvironment that predisposes susceptible patients to osteonecrosis, particularly when antiresorptive therapy suppresses bone turnover [1112]. In addition, severe periodontal breakdown often necessitates tooth extraction, which can directly trigger MRONJ and thereby confound the relationship between the PD process and the onset of necrosis [131415].

Despite this biological rationale, observational evidence on the magnitude of this association has been inconsistent [161718]. Several studies have identified PD as a significant predictor of MRONJ with high-risk estimates, whereas others have reported non-significant associations or findings limited by wide confidence intervals (CIs) and small sample sizes. For example, Walter et al. [19] reported a strong positive association in a case-control study, whereas Estilo et al. [20] found no significant correlation between radiographic alveolar bone loss and MRONJ. These discrepancies may reflect differences in study design, population characteristics, and, importantly, heterogeneity in the diagnostic criteria used to define PD severity.

Therefore, this systematic review and meta-analysis quantitatively synthesized the available evidence on the overall risk of MRONJ in patients with PD. We also stratified the analysis by disease severity, distinguishing severe periodontal breakdown from moderate-to-mixed disease, to examine potential severity-response patterns. Through this approach, we aimed to provide more precise evidence to guide dental management in patients receiving antiresorptive therapy.

sec.title: MATERIALS AND METHODS
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [21]. A protocol was established a priori to investigate the association between PD severity and MRONJ risk.

sec.title: Eligibility criteria
sec.p: The eligibility criteria for study selection were defined according to the population, exposure, comparator, and outcome (PECO) framework.

list-item.p: ▪ Population (P): Adult patients receiving antiresorptive agents, antiangiogenic agents, or other medications associated with MRONJ.

• Antiresorptive agents: These included long-term bisphosphonate therapy, such as zoledronic acid (Zometa® and Reclast®), pamidronate (Aredia®), alendronate (Fosamax®), ibandronate (Boniva®), risedronate (Actonel® and Atelvia®), etidronate (Didronel®), and tiludronate (Skelid®), as well as receptor activator of nuclear factor κB ligand inhibitors, such as denosumab (Xgeva® and Prolia®).

• Antiangiogenic agents: Cancer therapeutics that target angiogenesis also contribute to MRONJ risk. These include tyrosine kinase inhibitors, such as sunitinib (Sutent®) and sorafenib (Nexavar®); monoclonal antibodies against vascular endothelial growth factor, such as bevacizumab (Avastin®); and mammalian target of rapamycin pathway inhibitors, such as everolimus (Afinitor®).

• Other medications: Several newer agents have been reported to induce MRONJ in rare cases, including certain immunomodulatory or targeted therapies, such as neutralizing antibodies against tumor necrosis factor alpha or CD20, the anti-sclerostin antibody romosozumab (Evenity®), and other molecularly targeted drugs [22].

▪ Exposure (E): PD was required to be defined using reproducible clinical criteria, such as clinical attachment loss and probing pocket depth; radiographic criteria, such as alveolar bone loss; guideline-based criteria; or predefined administrative diagnostic/procedure-code criteria. Administrative-code definitions were accepted as indirect, record-based exposure definitions but were not considered equivalent to standardized clinical periodontal examination. Studies without operational diagnostic criteria, including those based on unspecified “clinical assessment” or unvalidated self-reported PD, were excluded.
▪ Comparator (C): Patients with clinically healthy periodontium or only mild periodontal conditions served as the non-exposed control group.

▪ Outcome (O): The outcome was development of MRONJ, defined as incidence or prevalence according to the American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons (AAOMS) or American Society for Bone and Mineral Research criteria. Studies reporting quantifiable effect estimates, including risk ratios (RRs), odds ratios (ORs), or hazard ratios (HRs), with 95% CIs were included.

sec.p: Exclusion criteria: Case reports, case series with n<10, reviews, animal studies, and studies lacking clear diagnostic criteria for PD, including self-reported surveys without clinical validation, were excluded.

sec.title: Search strategy and study selection
sec.p: Two authors (Jae-Hong Lee and Yun-Jeong Kim) independently conducted comprehensive electronic and manual literature searches of major databases, including MEDLINE via PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, and Google Scholar. The electronic search included studies published up to November 30, 2025, and used a combination of Medical Subject Headings terms, including “periodontitis,” “periodontal disease,” “gingivitis,” “oral health,” “tooth loss,” “antiresorptive,” “antiangiogenic,” “BRONJ,” “MRONJ,” “medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw,” “bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw,” and “osteonecrosis,” together with free-text keywords connected using Boolean operators (“AND” and “OR”).

sec.title: Data extraction and severity stratification
sec.p: Extracted data included study design, sample size, PD diagnostic criteria, and effect estimates. To address heterogeneity in PD definitions, studies were stratified into 2 subgroups according to the inferred severity reported in the primary studies [232425].

list-item.p: ▪ Severe/procedure-linked group: This group was defined using strict criteria indicative of advanced periodontal breakdown, including (1) radiographic evidence of alveolar bone loss and/or clinical attachment loss ≥5 mm or involving ≥1/3 of the root length, (2) a Community Periodontal Index (CPI) score of 4, defined as probing pocket depth ≥6 mm, or (3) PD necessitating tooth extraction. Administrative-code studies were not assumed to represent standardized clinical periodontal examination; when such studies combined a PD diagnostic code with a tooth-extraction procedure claim, they were interpreted as procedure-linked proxies for clinically advanced or treatment-requiring PD.

▪ Moderate-to-mixed group: This group was defined using broader diagnostic frameworks, including clinical assessments based on European Federation of Periodontology guidelines, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/American Academy of Periodontology definitions, CPI scores of 3–4, or radiographic bone loss ≥25%.

sec.p: The risk of bias in observational studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), with scores of 7–9 considered indicative of high quality [26]. To address the potential impact of implant-related MRONJ, we re-evaluated precipitating events in all primary studies. Implant-related outcomes were categorized as explicitly reported, not reported, or non-separable, such as outcomes grouped with tooth extractions. Because the lack of patient-level data precluded exclusion of individual cases, we conducted a conservative study-level sensitivity analysis by excluding entire studies that contained explicitly identifiable or non-separable implant-related MRONJ events (Table 1).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The meta-analysis was conducted using the generic inverse-variance method with log-transformed effect estimates and standard errors. Under the rare-outcome setting of MRONJ, RRs and ORs were treated as approximately comparable measures of relative association, whereas HRs were included more cautiously because they reflect time-to-event risk and are not mathematically identical to ORs or RRs. Sensitivity analyses excluding non-OR estimates were therefore performed. To further characterize between-study variation, a 95% prediction interval for the overall random-effects estimate was calculated on the log scale and back-transformed to the relative-effect scale. As a complementary assessment of small-study effects, Duval and Tweedie trim-and-fill analysis was performed using the L0 estimator under the same random-effects generic inverse-variance model. Because clinical and methodological heterogeneity was anticipated across studies, particularly in PD definitions, pooled relative-effect estimates and 95% CIs were estimated using a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model. Subgroup analyses were performed according to inferred PD severity, and heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic. All tests were 2-tailed, with statistical significance set at P<0.05.

sec.title: Literature search outcomes and quality assessment
sec.p: Overall, 3,114 records were identified using the search strategy. After 2,502 duplicate records were removed, 612 records were screened; 588 were excluded during title and abstract screening, and 24 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Ultimately, 8 observational studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in the quantitative synthesis, as summarized in the PRISMA flow diagram (Figure 1) and Table 2 [619202728293031]. Quality assessment of the 8 included observational studies indicated generally high methodological quality, with NOS scores ranging from 7 to 9 (Table 3).

In this retrospective single-center study, severe PD was identified as a significant independent risk factor for MRONJ (adjusted OR, 4.56), but the generalizability of these findings is limited by the small sample size and low number of events.
KCD-7 PD diagnostic code + tooth-extraction procedure claim

This nationwide claims-based study showed that MRONJ risk increased after tooth extraction among patients with a PD diagnostic code. Because the exposure was based on administrative billing records rather than standardized periodontal examination, this estimate was interpreted as a reproducible but indirect procedure-linked proxy of clinically advanced or treatment-requiring PD. Risk increased when PD progressed to the point of requiring extraction (HR, 2.55) compared with PD alone (HR, 1.68).

The absence of a statistically significant association between radiographic alveolar bone loss and MRONJ should be interpreted cautiously because this retrospective finding differs from the prevailing hypothesis that poor oral health is a predisposing risk factor.

The adjusted OR of 2.95 suggests a potential positive association between CDC/AAP-defined PD and MRONJ. However, this specific finding was not statistically significant and warrants cautious interpretation because the wide CI spans unity, unlike other significant clinical parameters identified in the study.

The validity of the findings is constrained by the retrospective case-control design and potential selection bias, particularly because the absence of CPI score 4 in the MRONJ group likely reflects prior extraction of severely compromised teeth rather than better periodontal health.

PD was identified as a statistically significant risk factor for MRONJ onset in denosumab-treated patients. However, the wide CI indicates uncertainty regarding the precise magnitude of risk, requiring cautious interpretation because of potential sample size limitations.

sec.title: Primary outcome
sec.p: The primary meta-analysis showed a robust, statistically significant association between PD and the risk of developing MRONJ. The overall pooled relative-effect estimate was 3.02 (95% CI, 1.99–4.56; P<0.001; I2=21.7%), indicating that patients with PD had an approximately threefold higher risk of MRONJ than those without PD. Statistical heterogeneity across the included studies was low, suggesting that the association was generally consistent across study designs and populations (Figure 2).

sec.title: Subgroup analysis by PD severity
sec.p: To explore potential sources of clinical heterogeneity, subgroup analysis was performed according to inferred PD severity. The severe/procedure-linked group, comprising 4 studies with stricter definitions such as extensive bone loss or PD requiring extraction, had a pooled relative-effect estimate of 4.26 (95% CI, 1.96–9.24; P<0.001; I2=43.4%) [6192728]. By comparison, the moderate-to-mixed group, which included 4 studies using broader diagnostic criteria, had a pooled relative-effect estimate of 2.39 (95% CI, 1.45–3.94; P<0.001; I2=0.0%) [20293031]. The formal test for subgroup differences was not statistically significant (P=0.267). Therefore, the higher point estimate in the severe/procedure-linked group should be interpreted cautiously as an exploratory finding rather than definitive evidence of a severity-response relationship.

sec.title: Heterogeneity and publication bias
sec.p: The overall analysis showed low-to-moderate heterogeneity (I2=21.7%; P=0.257). The moderate-to-mixed group showed no observed heterogeneity (I2=0.0%; P=0.494), whereas the severe/procedure-linked group showed moderate heterogeneity (I2=43.4%; P=0.151), likely reflecting differences in clinical, radiographic, and administrative exposure definitions. The 95% prediction interval for the overall pooled relative-effect estimate was 1.29–7.04, indicating that the predicted true effect in a future comparable study would remain above unity, although the interval was wider than the CI because it incorporates between-study variation. Because only 8 studies were included, formal assessment of publication bias was considered to have limited interpretability. The Egger regression test did not indicate marked small-study effects (P=0.496; Figure 3). Duval and Tweedie trim-and-fill analysis did not impute any missing studies (k0=0); therefore, the trim-and-fill adjusted estimate was unchanged from the primary analysis (pooled relative-effect estimate, 3.02; 95% CI, 1.99–4.56).

sec.title: Sensitivity analyses
sec.p: Sensitivity analyses were performed to assess whether the primary findings were influenced by individual studies, the largest study-specific effect estimate, inclusion of non-OR estimates, indirect exposure ascertainment, or inclusion of a pre-2014 BRONJ-era study. The severe/procedure-linked subgroup included 4 studies and had a pooled relative-effect estimate of 4.26 (95% CI, 1.96–9.24; I2=43.4%). In leave-one-out analysis, exclusion of Walter et al. [19], which contributed the largest study-specific estimate, attenuated the severe/procedure-linked subgroup estimate to 2.82 (95% CI, 1.66–4.77; I2=0.0%). Exclusion of Kwoen et al. [28], the only HR-based study and the only study using an administrative claims-based PD definition, yielded a subgroup estimate of 6.67 (95% CI, 2.93–15.21; I2=0.0%). This upward shift was expected because excluding Kwoen et al. [28], which reported the lowest subgroup estimate (HR, 2.55), shifted the summary estimate toward the remaining studies with higher effect estimates. This increase therefore reflects a methodological artifact related to the small subgroup size and study weighting rather than a true strengthening of the causal effect. When both Walter et al. [19] and Kwoen et al. [28] were excluded, the subgroup association remained statistically significant but imprecise because only 2 studies remained (pooled estimate, 4.00; 95% CI, 1.31–12.28; I2=0.0%).

At the overall meta-analysis level, exclusion of Walter et al. [19] yielded a pooled relative-effect estimate of 2.58 (95% CI, 1.80–3.71; I2=0.0%), whereas exclusion of Kwoen et al. [28] yielded a pooled estimate of 3.24 (95% CI, 1.91–5.51; I2=30.4%). An OR-only sensitivity analysis excluding Yamazaki et al. [6] and Kwoen et al. [28] yielded a pooled relative-effect estimate of 3.29 (95% CI, 1.82–5.93; I2=41.9%). An additional sensitivity analysis was conducted to address the inclusion of Estilo et al. [20], which used BRONJ-era terminology before the 2014 expansion of the MRONJ nomenclature. Exclusion of Estilo et al. [20] did not attenuate the association, yielding an overall pooled estimate of 3.24 (95% CI, 2.25–4.68; I2=0.0%) and a moderate-to-mixed subgroup estimate of 2.88 (95% CI, 1.64–5.04; I2=0.0%). Exclusion of both Walter et al. [19] and Kwoen et al. [28] yielded a pooled estimate of 2.61 (95% CI, 1.65–4.11; I2=0.0%).

To evaluate whether implant-related outcome mixing influenced the pooled association, conservative sensitivity analyses were performed. Exclusion of Kos [30] yielded a pooled relative-effect estimate of 2.97 (95% CI, 1.82–4.84; I2=31.3%). A further conservative analysis excluding both Kos [30] and Estilo et al. [20] yielded a pooled relative-effect estimate of 3.33 (95% CI, 2.11–5.26; I2=15.5%). Thus, the overall association between PD and MRONJ remained statistically significant after studies with explicitly identifiable or potentially non-separable implant-related outcome events were excluded.

sec.title: Impact of PD severity
sec.p: Our stratified analysis showed a numerically higher pooled estimate in studies that used strict clinical and/or radiographic definitions or procedure-linked proxies of advanced PD. This pattern is clinically plausible because advanced periodontal breakdown or extraction-requiring PD may reflect greater inflammatory burden, infection, and treatment complexity. However, the subgroup difference was not statistically significant, and 1 study in this subgroup used administrative claims data rather than standardized periodontal examination. Therefore, these findings should not be interpreted as definitive evidence of a severity-response gradient. Instead, they suggest that more advanced or procedure-linked PD definitions may identify patients at higher clinical risk, a hypothesis that requires confirmation in future studies using standardized periodontal diagnostic criteria.

Importantly, the association observed in this meta-analysis should not be interpreted as evidence of a direct independent effect of periodontal inflammation on MRONJ development. In medication-exposed patients, severe PD often leads to invasive dentoalveolar treatment, particularly tooth extraction, which is itself a well-established precipitating trigger of MRONJ; in some cases, implant-related procedures may also contribute. Consistent with the 2022 AAOMS position paper [1], preexisting inflammatory dental disease may confound the relationship between tooth extraction and MRONJ, and extraction may sometimes expose preexisting disease rather than act as the sole precipitating event. Therefore, the observed association likely reflects a combination of preexisting inflammatory burden and downstream procedure-related pathways rather than a single isolated mechanism.

Implant-related MRONJ represents a distinct clinical pathway and should not be conflated with PD- or tooth-extraction-related MRONJ. Therefore, the primary studies were re-examined for implant-related outcome reporting. This audit showed that Kos [30] explicitly reported 1 implant-insertion-related BRONJ case, whereas Estilo et al. [20] reported dental extraction/dental implant placement as a combined, non-separable category. Conservative sensitivity analyses excluding Kos [30] alone, and then excluding both Kos [30] and Estilo et al. [20], did not materially alter the overall association (pooled relative-effect estimates, 2.97 and 3.33, respectively). These findings suggest that the primary association was not driven by identifiable or potentially non-separable implant-related MRONJ events. However, because trigger-specific patient-level data were unavailable in most primary studies, residual outcome mixing among periodontal, extraction-related, implant-related, and spontaneous MRONJ pathways cannot be fully excluded.

sec.title: Biological plausibility linking PD and MRONJ
sec.p: The pathogenesis of MRONJ remains incompletely understood and is widely considered to be multifactorial [32]. A central concept is that MRONJ arises from an imbalance between bone injury and repair, exacerbated by pharmacologic suppression of normal healing mechanisms. Antiresorptive agents inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone remodeling and limit microdamage repair, whereas antiangiogenic agents impair vascularization and nutrient delivery. When these pharmacological factors coincide with local insults, such as infection or mechanical trauma, the jawbone may become particularly susceptible to osteonecrosis. Experimental models have shown that bisphosphonate administration in the presence of local inflammation, including post-extraction or mucosal injury, can reproduce MRONJ-like lesions, supporting the role of inflammatory triggers in disease development [3334]. Not all patients with oral infections develop MRONJ; however, risk increases markedly in the presence of systemic compromise or comorbidities.

Oral microbiota likely contribute to MRONJ progression, but the available evidence does not support attribution of the condition to a single specific microorganism [3536]. Although Actinomyces is frequently detected in MRONJ lesions, this finding should be interpreted cautiously [37]. Actinomyces is part of the normal oral biofilm ecology and is not typically regarded as a principal high-virulence periodontal pathogen comparable to the classic red-complex taxa [3839]. In MRONJ, its presence may reflect opportunistic or secondary colonization of exposed necrotic bone and persistence within biofilm-rich lesions rather than a primary initiating cause [374041]. Therefore, the relevance of Actinomyces in MRONJ should be understood as a lesion-associated microbiological finding with possible implications for chronic infection and delayed healing, rather than as evidence of a direct shared pathogenic pathway between periodontitis and MRONJ.

From the periodontal perspective, clear parallels exist between MRONJ and chronic PD. Both conditions are characterized by microbial dysbiosis, persistent inflammation, and compromised bone homeostasis. Evidence suggests that the dysregulated oral microbiome in patients with MRONJ contributes to pathological inflammation and impaired bone healing [36]. Notably, PD and peri-implantitis share key hallmarks with MRONJ lesions, including persistent inflammation and delayed tissue regeneration, suggesting that similar pathogenic pathways may be involved [3542]. Periodontal pathogens release lipopolysaccharides and other virulence factors that stimulate inflammatory cytokine production and osteoclast activity. When normal reparative capacity is suppressed by antiresorptive therapy, these processes may contribute to progressive bone damage. In addition, local infection in the periodontal pocket can reduce the pH of the surrounding bone marrow and gingival tissues, thereby undermining bone matrix integrity and drug binding [4344]. Under physiological conditions, the jawbone and oral mucosa serve as effective barriers to microbial invasion. However, these protective functions are compromised in patients receiving MRONJ-associated medications, increasing susceptibility to opportunistic bone infection by oral microorganisms.

The observed association between PD and MRONJ is biologically plausible; however, it should not be interpreted as evidence of a confirmed causal mechanism. Chronic periodontal inflammation, microbial dysbiosis, and local tissue breakdown may contribute to an oral environment that is less favorable for healing in patients receiving antiresorptive or antiangiogenic therapy. However, the present meta-analysis cannot determine whether these factors are directly causal, whether they act through extraction or other intermediates, or whether the association is partly explained by residual confounding. Therefore, the mechanistic considerations discussed here should be regarded as plausible hypotheses that contextualize the observed association rather than as causal conclusions.

sec.title: Preventive strategies for MRONJ from a periodontal perspective
sec.p: Current clinical consensus consistently recognizes prevention as the most effective approach to MRONJ management [1]. Given established systemic and local risk factors, patients receiving antiresorptive or antiangiogenic therapy require structured periodontal care to reduce oral inflammatory burden and limit potential sources of infection or trauma. Importantly, concern about MRONJ should not lead to postponement or neglect of periodontal treatment. Inadequately controlled periodontal inflammation may itself increase susceptibility to MRONJ.
Based on the available evidence and existing guideline frameworks, the following preventive strategies are proposed for patients at increased risk of MRONJ.

sec.title: Comprehensive periodontal evaluation before initiation of therapy
sec.p: A thorough periodontal assessment should be performed before high-risk medications are initiated. Teeth with unfavorable or questionable prognoses should be definitively managed, often through extraction or periodontal therapy, before antiresorptive or antiangiogenic treatment begins. The goal is to eliminate potential sites of infection and avoid the need for invasive periodontal procedures during medication therapy.

sec.title: Patient education and maintenance of periodontal health
sec.p: Patients should be educated about the importance of maintaining oral hygiene and encouraged to report periodontal symptoms promptly. Routine supportive periodontal therapy and effective daily plaque control are essential to limit disease progression. In high-risk cases, such as patients with cancer receiving intravenous bisphosphonates, shorter recall intervals of approximately 3–4 months with periodontal reassessment are advisable to enable early intervention.

sec.title: Prioritization of non-surgical periodontal therapy during medication exposure
sec.p: During antiresorptive or antiangiogenic treatment, elective dentoalveolar surgery should be avoided whenever feasible. In patients with PD, non-surgical periodontal therapy, including scaling, root planing, and frequent supportive periodontal therapy, should be prioritized over surgical approaches when clinically appropriate [2]. Non-surgical periodontal treatment can substantially reduce periodontal bacterial load and inflammation while carrying a much lower risk of bone exposure, thereby lowering the risk of MRONJ.

sec.title: Risk mitigation when invasive procedures are unavoidable
sec.p: When an invasive dental procedure is unavoidable, such as extraction of a hopeless tooth or clearly indicated periodontal surgery, clinicians should take steps to minimize MRONJ risk. Experts commonly recommend antibiotic prophylaxis at the time of dental extraction or periodontal surgery for patients at high risk [4546]. Close postoperative monitoring is essential until complete mucosal healing is achieved. Delayed healing or signs of bone exposure should prompt immediate clinical evaluation.

sec.title: Interdisciplinary coordination of care
sec.p: Prevention and management of MRONJ require close collaboration between dental and medical teams. Coordination among periodontists, oral surgeons, prescribing physicians, and other healthcare professionals is critical to optimize treatment timing, reinforce patient education, and ensure continuity of care throughout pharmacological therapy.

Collectively, these consensus-based strategies emphasize the central role of periodontal care in MRONJ prevention. Avoiding periodontal treatment may paradoxically increase risk by allowing chronic inflammation and infection to persist. Proactive, individualized periodontal management focused on inflammation control and disease stabilization should therefore be considered an essential component of MRONJ risk reduction.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. First, the number of included studies was relatively small, limiting the certainty of the evidence, particularly for subgroup analyses. In particular, the severe/procedure-linked subgroup included only 4 studies, and sensitivity analyses showed that, although the direction of the association was generally consistent, the magnitude of the pooled estimate was influenced by individual studies. Second, heterogeneity in PD definitions across studies may have introduced exposure misclassification. Third, because most included studies were retrospective, selection bias, incomplete confounder adjustment, and residual confounding cannot be excluded. Fourth, precipitating events such as tooth extraction, implant placement, and spontaneous onset were not consistently reported or adjusted for; thus, the pooled estimate should be interpreted as reflecting the total clinical association between PD and MRONJ rather than a direct independent inflammatory effect. Fifth, combining ORs, HRs, and RRs under the rare-outcome assumption remains an approximation. Finally, the small number of studies limits the reliability of publication-bias and heterogeneity assessments. These limitations underscore the need for cautious interpretation, and future studies with standardized definitions and better adjustment for procedural and clinical confounders are warranted to validate the findings.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: Current evidence supports PD as a clinically relevant factor associated with MRONJ risk in patients receiving antiresorptive or antiangiogenic therapy. Although the overall association was generally consistent, the limited number of studies and the potential contribution of procedure-related pathways, particularly tooth extraction, warrant cautious interpretation. Although more advanced periodontal breakdown may be associated with higher risk, this finding remains exploratory and should not be interpreted as proof of a direct independent inflammatory effect. These findings support comprehensive periodontal assessment and stabilization as part of MRONJ risk-reduction strategies.
